title: Molecules are springs
key_message: The stiffer the bond and the lighter the atoms, the higher the frequency: so C–H is on the left, C–Cl on the right.
body: Imagine two balls joined by a spring. If the spring is stiff or the balls are light, they vibrate quickly; if the spring is soft or the balls are heavy, they vibrate slowly. In molecules it is the same: a bond to hydrogen (light) vibrates fast and sits on the left of the spectrum; a C=O double bond (stiff) sits in the middle; bonds to heavy atoms sit on the right.
Try it: move the sliders or pick a bond and watch how the [[wavenumber|wavenumber]] changes. The model predicts the order of the bands, not the exact value.
for_chemists: [[harmonic-oscillator|Harmonic oscillator]]: ν̃ = (1/2πc)·√(k/μ), with the [[reduced-mass|reduced mass]] μ = m₁m₂/(m₁+m₂) and the [[force-constant|force constant]] k. With k in N/m and μ in u, ν̃ ≈ 130.3·√(k/μ) cm⁻¹. C–H example: k ≈ 500 N/m, μ = 0.93 u, ν̃ ≈ 3020 cm⁻¹ against 2850–2960 observed.

Replacing H with D lowers ν̃ by the factor √(μ_D/μ_H): for O–H and O–D it is about 1.37, not √2. The k values in the figure are orders of magnitude from teaching literature, not measurements; the model predicts the order (C≡N > C=O > C–C, X–H on top), not the exact value. F–H falls above C–H despite the slightly larger reduced mass: the increase in k matters more.
The real potential is not a parabola ([[anharmonicity|anharmonicity]]): levels get closer as they go up and the first [[overtone|overtone]] falls a little below twice the fundamental.

figure.alt: Two balls joined by a zigzag spring. The dashed outline shows the extreme position of the vibration; the heavier ball moves less.
